chapters.title: Israel’s fighting men are numbered

parts.text: In the wilderness of Sinai, the LORD commands Moses and Aaron to count Israel’s men aged twenty and above who are able to go to war. Named leaders from each tribe assist them. The people declare their families and ancestry, and the chapter records the number from each tribe, treating Ephraim and Manasseh separately. The total is 603,550 men.

The Levites are not included in this military census. Instead, God appoints them over the tabernacle, its furnishings, transport, and service. They must camp around it and guard it from unauthorized approach. The other Israelites camp by their own companies and standards, while the Levites’ position helps keep wrath from falling upon the congregation.

chapters.title: The order of Israel’s camp and march

parts.text: The LORD assigns Israel’s tribes their positions around the tabernacle, each under its standard and family signs. Judah camps on the east with Issachar and Zebulun and leads the march. Reuben camps on the south with Simeon and Gad and follows second. The tabernacle and the Levites travel in the middle, maintaining their appointed place among the camps.

Ephraim camps on the west with Manasseh and Benjamin and marches third among the tribal divisions. Dan camps on the north with Asher and Naphtali and brings up the rear. The chapter records each division’s numbers and repeats the total of 603,550, excluding the Levites. Israel follows the LORD’s directions in both camping and travelling.

chapters.title: The Levites serve in place of the firstborn

parts.text: The chapter names Aaron’s sons and recalls the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, leaving Eleazar and Ithamar to minister as priests. God gives the Levites to assist Aaron, guard the sanctuary’s service, and stand in place of Israel’s firstborn, whom he claimed when striking Egypt. Levi’s males are counted from one month old. Gershon’s families camp west of the tabernacle and care for its curtains and coverings.

Kohath’s families camp south and care for the sacred furnishings, while Merari’s families camp north and handle the framework and fittings. Moses, Aaron, and Aaron’s sons camp east. Israel’s firstborn are counted, and those exceeding the number of Levites are redeemed with money. Moses gives this redemption payment to Aaron and his sons.

chapters.title: The Levites’ duties in transporting the sanctuary

parts.text: God numbers the Kohathites aged thirty to fifty for tabernacle service. Before they carry the holy furnishings, Aaron and his sons must cover and prepare each item according to prescribed arrangements. The Kohathites must neither touch the holy things nor enter to watch them being covered, lest they die. Eleazar oversees the oil, incense, continual meat offering, and sanctuary equipment.

The Gershonites transport curtains, coverings, hangings, and related cords under Ithamar’s direction. The Merarites carry boards, bars, pillars, sockets, and associated fittings, with individual responsibilities assigned. Moses, Aaron, and the leaders count the eligible men of all three families. Their combined service force totals 8,580, each appointed to his particular work and burden.

chapters.title: Purity, restitution, and suspected unfaithfulness

parts.text: The LORD commands that people with leprosy, bodily discharges, or uncleanness from the dead be put outside the camp, where he dwells among Israel. Those who wrong another person must confess, repay the loss, and add a fifth. If no relative can receive restitution, it goes to the priest along with the required atonement offering. Holy contributions also belong to the priest.

A further law addresses a husband’s jealousy when he suspects his wife of adultery but lacks witnesses. He brings her and a prescribed offering to the priest. She stands before the LORD under an oath and drinks the appointed water. The ceremony places the determination before God, distinguishing a guilty woman from an innocent one rather than treating suspicion itself as proof.

chapters.title: The Nazarite vow and the priestly blessing

parts.text: A man or woman may make a special Nazarite vow of separation to the LORD. During the vow, the person avoids wine and all grape products, lets the hair grow, and does not approach a dead body even for a close relative. If sudden contact with death defiles the vow, cleansing, sacrifices, and a new period of separation are required; the previous days do not count.

When the vow is completed, prescribed offerings are brought, the consecrated hair is shaved and burned with the peace offering, and the priest performs the appointed rites. The LORD then gives Aaron and his sons words with which to bless Israel, asking for God’s protection, gracious favour, and peace. They place his name upon the people, and he promises to bless them.

chapters.title: The tribal leaders dedicate the altar

parts.text: At the tabernacle’s dedication, Israel’s leaders bring six covered wagons and twelve oxen. Moses distributes them to the Gershonites and Merarites according to their transport duties; the Kohathites receive none because they carry the holy things on their shoulders. Each tribal leader also brings an offering for the altar’s dedication on a separate day, beginning with Nahshon of Judah.

For twelve days the leaders present equal gifts: silver vessels filled with flour and oil, a gold spoon of incense, and animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings. The repeated account names each tribe and its representative, then totals the gifts. When Moses enters the tabernacle, he hears God speaking from above the mercy seat between the cherubims.

chapters.title: The Levites are cleansed and presented for service

parts.text: God directs Aaron to arrange the seven lamps so they give light before the candlestick, which was made according to the pattern shown to Moses. The Levites are then prepared for service through purification, washing, shaving, and sacrifices. Israel gathers and lays hands on them, and Aaron presents them before the LORD as an offering from the people.

The LORD takes the Levites in place of Israel’s firstborn and gives them to Aaron and his sons to serve the congregation and guard against a plague arising from unauthorized approach. Moses and Aaron carry out the cleansing and presentation. The chapter assigns entry into service at twenty-five and withdrawal from its regular labour at fifty, while allowing continued assistance in keeping the charge.

chapters.title: passover provision and guidance by the cloud

parts.text: Israel keeps the passover in the wilderness during the second year after leaving Egypt. Men unclean through contact with a dead body ask how they may participate. God permits those unclean or away on a journey to observe it in the second month, following the same meal regulations. A clean person who simply neglects the feast bears guilt. The same rule applies to resident strangers.

The cloud covers the tabernacle by day, appearing like fire at night. Whenever it rises, Israel journeys, and wherever it settles, they camp. Whether it remains for a night, several days, a month, or longer, the people wait for the LORD’s command. Their movement and rest are governed by his direction through the cloud.

chapters.title: Trumpets and the departure from Sinai

parts.text: God commands two silver trumpets for summoning the congregation and directing the camps’ movements. Different signals gather all the people, summon leaders, or begin the march. Aaron’s sons are to blow them. Trumpets also accompany war, days of rejoicing, appointed feasts, and new moons, serving as a memorial before the LORD over Israel’s sacrifices.

In the second month of the second year, the cloud rises and Israel leaves Sinai in the appointed order. The Levites carry the tabernacle and its furnishings between the tribal divisions. Moses asks Hobab to accompany them and share God’s promised goodness. The ark goes before them to seek a resting place, and Moses speaks prayers at its setting out and resting.

chapters.title: Craving meat and sharing Moses’ burden

parts.text: The people complain, and fire from the LORD burns at the camp’s edge until Moses prays. Then the mixed multitude and Israel crave meat and remember Egypt’s food with longing, despising the manna. Overwhelmed, Moses tells God that he cannot bear the people alone. God commands seventy elders to share his burden and promises so much meat that it will become loathsome because the people have rejected him.

God places his Spirit upon the elders, who prophesy. When Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp, Moses welcomes the news rather than guarding his own position. A wind brings abundant quails, which the people eagerly gather. While the meat is still in their mouths, a great plague strikes, and the place is named for the graves of those who lusted.

chapters.title: Miriam and Aaron challenge Moses

parts.text: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over his Ethiopian wife and question whether God speaks only through him. The chapter describes Moses as very meek. God summons all three to the tabernacle and explains that he ordinarily makes himself known to prophets in visions and dreams, but speaks with Moses more directly. He rebukes them for speaking against his faithful servant.

When the cloud departs, Miriam is leprous. Aaron admits their foolish sin and pleads with Moses not to let her suffer like one dead. Moses cries to God for her healing. God requires her to remain outside the camp seven days, after which she may return. Israel waits until she is restored before continuing its journey.

chapters.title: The spies inspect Canaan

parts.text: At the LORD’s command, Moses sends one leader from each tribe to inspect Canaan. The chapter names them, including Caleb and Oshea, whom Moses calls Jehoshua (Joshua). They must examine the people, cities, soil, and produce and bring back fruit. Their mission is to report on the land and its inhabitants as Israel approaches the inheritance God has promised.

After forty days, the men return with fruit, including a large cluster of grapes from Eshcol. They confirm that the land flows with milk and honey but describe strong inhabitants and fortified cities. Caleb urges immediate possession, confident they can overcome it. The other men oppose him, spread an evil report, and describe themselves as grasshoppers beside the giants they saw.

chapters.title: Unbelief leads to forty years in the wilderness

parts.text: Israel mourns the spies’ report, wishes it had died in Egypt, and proposes choosing a leader to return there. Joshua and Caleb insist that the land is good and that the LORD can give it to them, but the people threaten to stone them. God’s glory appears. Moses pleads against destroying Israel, appealing to God’s reputation, mercy, and faithfulness. God pardons at Moses’ request but declares that the unbelieving generation will not see the land.

Those numbered from twenty years old who murmured will die in the wilderness, except Caleb and Joshua. Their children will enter after forty years corresponding to the spies’ forty days. The men who spread the evil report die by plague. Israel then attempts an invasion against Moses’ warning and without the LORD’s presence, and suffers defeat.

chapters.title: Offerings, defiant sin, and remembrance

parts.text: God gives Israel instructions for grain and drink offerings to accompany animal sacrifices when they enter the land. Quantities vary with the animal offered, and the same law applies to Israelites and resident strangers. The first portion of dough is to be offered to the LORD. Atonement is provided when the congregation or an individual sins through ignorance.

Deliberate, defiant sin is distinguished from ignorance: the person who despises the LORD’s word is cut off and bears guilt. A man found gathering sticks on the sabbath is held until God commands his execution, which the congregation carries out. Finally, Israel is told to wear fringes with a blue ribbon, reminding them to keep God’s commandments rather than follow their own hearts and eyes.

chapters.title: Korah’s rebellion and Aaron’s intervention

parts.text: Korah and other leaders challenge Moses and Aaron, claiming the whole congregation’s holiness. Moses declares that God will show whom he has chosen and rebukes the demand for priestly office. Dathan and Abiram refuse his summons and accuse him of failed leadership. As the assembly confronts Moses and Aaron, God warns the people away from the rebels. The earth swallows Dathan and Abiram, their households, all the men that appertained unto Korah, and their goods. Fire consumes the 250 incense-offering men.

Their censers become a covering for the altar, warning against unauthorized priesthood. The next day the people blame Moses and Aaron for the deaths, and a plague begins. Aaron runs among them with incense and makes atonement, standing between the dead and living until the plague stops. Another 14,700 have died.

chapters.title: Aaron’s rod blossoms

parts.text: To end Israel’s complaints about the priesthood, the LORD commands each tribal leader to provide a rod bearing his name, with Aaron’s name on Levi’s rod. Moses places them before the testimony in the tabernacle. God says the rod of the man he chooses will blossom. The next day Aaron’s rod has sprouted buds, produced blossoms, and yielded almonds. The leaders see it and take back their rods.

God commands Moses to keep Aaron’s rod before the testimony as a warning against rebellion, so the people’s complaints will not bring death. Alarmed by the recent judgments and this sign, the Israelites express fear that approaching the LORD’s tabernacle will lead to their destruction.

chapters.title: Priestly responsibility and provision for the Levites

parts.text: The LORD assigns Aaron and his sons responsibility for the sanctuary and priesthood, with the Levites assisting but forbidden to approach the holy vessels and altar as priests. Their careful service guards Israel against further wrath. God gives the priests portions of holy offerings, firstfruits, and redeemed firstborn as their provision. Aaron has no territorial inheritance like the other tribes: the LORD is his portion.

The Levites receive Israel’s tithes in return for their tabernacle service and likewise have no tribal land inheritance. From those tithes they must offer a tenth to the LORD, giving the best portion to Aaron the priest. What remains may support their households as wages for their work, provided they do not profane the holy gifts.

chapters.title: The red heifer and cleansing from death

parts.text: God prescribes an unblemished red heifer that has never borne a yoke. It is killed outside the camp under Eleazar’s supervision, and its blood is sprinkled toward the tabernacle. The whole animal is burned with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet. A clean person gathers the ashes for use in water of separation. Those involved in preparing them must wash and remain unclean until evening.

Contact with a human corpse makes a person unclean seven days. The prescribed water is applied on the third and seventh days, followed by washing. Rules cover deaths in tents, graves, bones, and open-field contact. Refusing purification defiles the sanctuary and brings exclusion from Israel. The chapter also addresses uncleanness passed through contact with an unclean person.

chapters.title: Water at Meribah, Edom’s refusal, and Aaron’s death

parts.text: Miriam dies and is buried at Kadesh. When the congregation lacks water, it quarrels with Moses and Aaron and longs for Egypt. God tells Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock before the people. Moses instead speaks angrily and strikes it twice. Water flows, but God declares that Moses and Aaron will not lead Israel into the land because they failed to believe and sanctify him before the people.

Moses requests peaceful passage through Edom, offering to pay for water, but Edom refuses and advances with an army. Israel turns away. On Mount Hor, Aaron’s priestly garments are transferred to Eleazar, and Aaron dies. The congregation mourns him for thirty days.

chapters.title: The brass serpent and victories east of Jordan

parts.text: After a Canaanite attack, Israel vows to devote the enemy’s cities to destruction, and the LORD grants victory. Later the people complain against God and Moses about the journey and food. Fiery serpents kill many, and the people confess their sin. God tells Moses to make a serpent and place it on a pole; those bitten live when they look at it. Israel then continues through the wilderness.

At a well provided by God, Israel sings as the princes dig. Sihon king of the Amorites refuses passage and attacks, but Israel defeats him and takes his cities, including Heshbon. Og king of Bashan also comes against them. God assures Moses, and Israel defeats Og and possesses his land.

chapters.title: Balak summons Balaam

parts.text: Alarmed by Israel’s approach, Balak king of Moab sends messengers with rewards to hire Balaam to curse them. God tells Balaam not to go or curse the people because they are blessed. Balak sends more honoured messengers with greater promises. Balaam says he cannot go beyond God’s word. God later permits him to accompany the men, but only to speak what he is commanded.

On the journey, God’s anger is kindled, and an angel blocks the road. Balaam’s ass sees the angel and repeatedly turns aside, receiving beatings. God enables the ass to speak and opens Balaam’s eyes. The angel warns him that his way is perverse. Balaam proceeds under renewed limits, meets Balak, and insists he can speak only what God gives him.

chapters.title: Balaam blesses those Balak wants cursed

parts.text: Balak and Balaam prepare seven altars and sacrifices. God meets Balaam and gives him a message: he cannot curse those God has not cursed. He describes Israel as a people dwelling apart, too numerous to count, and expresses a desire for the righteous person’s end. Balak protests that Balaam has blessed the very enemies he was hired to curse.

From another location they offer sacrifices again. Balaam declares that God does not lie or reverse his blessing like a man. God is with Israel, having brought them out of Egypt, and enchantments cannot overturn his purpose. Israel will rise with a lion’s strength. Frustrated, Balak takes Balaam to a third place and prepares another set of offerings.

chapters.title: Balaam’s final blessings and future sayings

parts.text: Seeing that God intends to bless Israel, Balaam no longer seeks enchantments but looks toward the camp. The Spirit of God comes upon him, and he speaks of Israel’s beautiful tents, abundant provision, exalted kingdom, and strength against enemies. Blessing and curse are attached to how others treat Israel. Balak angrily dismisses him, and Balaam repeats that he cannot speak contrary to the LORD for payment.

Balaam then speaks of what will happen in latter days: a Star and Sceptre arise from Israel, defeating Moab and taking possession of Edom. He also gives sayings concerning Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur, and ships from Chittim, describing coming conquest and destruction. Balaam and Balak then go their separate ways.

chapters.title: Baal-peor and Phinehas’ zeal

parts.text: At Shittim, Israelites join Moabite women in sexual immorality and sacrifices to their gods, attaching themselves to Baal-peor. The LORD’s anger is kindled, and Moses directs the judges to execute those joined to that worship. While the congregation weeps, an Israelite openly brings a Midianite woman among them. Phinehas follows and kills both, and the plague stops after twenty-four thousand deaths.

God declares that Phinehas turned away his wrath through zeal for God’s honour and grants him a covenant of peace and an enduring priesthood for his descendants. The slain pair are identified as Zimri, a Simeonite leader, and Cozbi, a Midianite ruler’s daughter. God commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies for their deceit in the matter of Peor.

chapters.title: A new generation is numbered

parts.text: After the plague, the LORD commands Moses and Eleazar to count Israel’s fighting men aged twenty and above. The chapter lists each tribe’s families and numbers, recording a total of 601,730. Genealogical notes recall the rebellion of Dathan and Abiram, state that Korah’s children did not die, and identify Zelophehad’s five daughters because he had no sons.

The land is to be divided among the tribes according to their numbers, with lots determining the allocation. Levite males are counted separately from one month old because they receive no territorial inheritance among Israel. The chapter emphasizes that the earlier wilderness census generation has died as the LORD declared; only Caleb and Joshua remain from those previously numbered.

chapters.title: Inheritance for daughters and Joshua’s appointment

parts.text: Zelophehad’s daughters ask for an inheritance because their father died without sons. They explain that he was not part of Korah’s company and appeal against losing his name from the family. Moses brings the matter before the LORD. God affirms their claim: when a man dies without a son, inheritance passes to his daughter. If there is no daughter, it passes successively to brothers, paternal uncles, and the nearest family relative as each earlier category is absent.

God tells Moses to view the promised land before his death, recalling his rebellion at Meribah. Moses asks for a leader so Israel will not be like sheep without a shepherd. God chooses Joshua, a man in whom is the spirit. Moses publicly lays hands on him and commissions him before Eleazar and the congregation.

chapters.title: Daily, weekly, monthly, and spring offerings

parts.text: The LORD commands Israel to present his offerings at their appointed times. Two unblemished lambs are offered daily, one in the morning and one in the evening, with grain and drink offerings. sabbath offerings are added to the continual sacrifice. Each new moon brings a larger burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings and a goat for sin.

The chapter prescribes sacrifices for passover’s accompanying feast of unleavened bread, with holy assemblies on the first and seventh days and restrictions on ordinary work. It also sets out the offerings for the feast of weeks, when new grain is brought. These festival sacrifices supplement rather than replace the continual daily offering, and the animals must be without blemish.

chapters.title: Offerings for the seventh-month feasts

parts.text: The LORD specifies offerings for the first day of the seventh month, a holy assembly marked by trumpet blowing. These are added to the regular daily and monthly sacrifices. On the tenth day, Israel must afflict their souls and refrain from work; the prescribed sacrifices accompany the day of atonement in addition to its special atoning offering and the daily service.

The feast beginning on the fifteenth day lasts seven days, followed by an eighth-day assembly. The number of bullocks decreases from thirteen on the first day to seven on the seventh, while the other prescribed offerings continue. The eighth day has its own sacrifices and rest. Moses delivers these requirements, which stand alongside Israel’s vows and voluntary gifts.

chapters.title: Vows and household responsibility

parts.text: Moses tells the tribal leaders that a man who vows to the LORD or binds himself by an oath must fulfil his word. A young woman living in her father’s house is likewise bound if her father hears and allows the vow, but he may disallow it when he hears. Similar provision applies when a woman enters marriage while under a vow.

A widow or divorced woman remains responsible for her vows. Within marriage, a husband may confirm his wife’s vow by allowing it or annul it when he first hears. Silence from day to day establishes it; if he later makes it void, he bears the iniquity. These rules distinguish personal obligations from the responsibilities of fathers and husbands within the household.

chapters.title: Judgment on Midian and division of the spoil

parts.text: God commands vengeance on Midian before Moses’ death. Twelve thousand Israelites fight under the accompanying ministry of Phinehas, killing the Midianite kings and Balaam and taking captives and spoil. Moses rebukes the officers for sparing women who, through Balaam’s counsel, had drawn Israel into the sin at Peor. He commands the killing of male children and women who have known men, while sparing young women who have not. Purification is required for soldiers, captives, and equipment.

The spoil is counted and divided between the warriors and congregation, with prescribed contributions for the LORD, the priest, and the Levites. The officers report that none of their men is missing. They bring captured gold as an offering, which is placed in the tabernacle as a memorial before the LORD.

chapters.title: Eastern land granted with a promise to fight

parts.text: Reuben and Gad request the fertile land east of Jordan because of their abundant livestock. Moses fears they will discourage the other tribes as the earlier spies did, bringing renewed wrath. They propose to settle their families and animals securely while their fighting men cross ahead of Israel and remain until the other tribes receive their inheritance.

Moses accepts the arrangement if they fulfil their promise before the LORD, warning that failure will be sin and that their sin will find them out. The agreement is stated before Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders. Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh receive the conquered eastern kingdoms, fortify towns, and establish settlements. The chapter also records additional conquests by Manasseh’s families.

chapters.title: Israel’s journeys and instructions for entering Canaan

parts.text: Moses records Israel’s stages of travel at the LORD’s command, tracing the route from Rameses after the passover through the wilderness to the plains of Moab. The list recalls departure while Egypt buried its firstborn, the crossing of the sea, places of water and hardship, and many encampments. It also records Aaron’s death on Mount Hor at 123 years old in the fortieth year.

In the plains of Moab, God commands Israel to drive out Canaan’s inhabitants, destroy their images and high places, and possess the land. The inheritance is to be distributed by lot according to family size. If Israel leaves inhabitants in place, they will become persistent sources of trouble, and God will do to Israel what he intended for those nations.

chapters.title: Canaan’s boundaries and appointed distributors

parts.text: The LORD defines the boundaries of the land Israel is to inherit in Canaan, describing its southern, western, northern, and eastern limits. The western boundary is the great sea, and the eastern boundary descends through the Sea of Chinnereth and Jordan to the salt sea. These borders define Israel’s promised inheritance.

Moses explains that this western territory is to be divided by lot among nine tribes and half a tribe, since Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh have already received land east of Jordan. God appoints Eleazar the priest and Joshua to oversee the division, assisted by a named leader from each participating tribe. Caleb is appointed for Judah among these representatives.

chapters.title: Levitical cities and refuge for manslayers

parts.text: Israel must give the Levites forty-eight cities with surrounding land for their animals, taking more from larger tribal inheritances and fewer from smaller ones. Six of these are cities of refuge, three on either side of Jordan. They provide protection for anyone who kills a person unintentionally until the case can be judged, including Israelites, strangers, and sojourners.

The law distinguishes murder from accidental killing by the weapon, intent, and circumstances. A murderer must be put to death on adequate witness testimony; one witness alone is insufficient. An accidental killer remains in the city of refuge until the high priest dies. No ransom may substitute for a murderer’s sentence or shorten that refuge requirement. Bloodshed must not pollute the land where the LORD dwells.

chapters.title: Preserving tribal inheritances

parts.text: Leaders of Manasseh’s families raise a concern about Zelophehad’s daughters: if they marry outside their tribe, their inherited land will pass to another tribe and remain transferred at jubile. Moses gives the LORD’s ruling that their concern is justified. The daughters may marry whom they choose, provided they marry within their father’s tribe, preserving the family inheritance.

This principle applies to every Israelite daughter who possesses an inheritance, so tribal holdings do not pass from one tribe to another through marriage. Zelophehad’s daughters obey and marry their father’s brothers’ sons within Manasseh. The book ends by identifying these as commandments and judgments given through Moses in the plains of Moab, beside Jordan near Jericho.
